newsitem.title: USA: Hun Sen coup probably spells end of some U.S. aid.
newsitem.headline: Hun Sen coup probably spells end of some U.S. aid.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it was unlikely to resume nonhumanitarian aid to Cambodia, where Second Prime Minister Hun Sen took sole control of the government in a coup nine days ago.
At a news briefing, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Hun Sen's rhetoric in recent days, seemingly in favour of democracy, was not matched by actions.
But he said Washington had "no direct evidence" that Hun Sen was involved in drug trafficking, as the man he ousted from power, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, has alleged.

In the wake of the coup, the United States last week suspended all bilateral aid to Cambodia for 30 days. Washington allocated $35 million in aid to the Southeast Asian state for fiscal 1997, which ends in September.

Anticipating what might happen after 30 days, Burns said, "I know that we would very much like to keep going, keep operational those portions of the aid programme that benefit people but not the government."
The attempt to rid Cambodia of land mines is one of those programmes.

But he added: "I don't think you'll see us embracing Hun Sen and giving him billions of dollars, or millions of dollars, for his own personal use. ... I don't anticipate you'll see a lot of government-to-government aid (from the United States to Cambodia)."

As for multilateral aid, which in recent years has made up about half of Cambodia's budget, Burns said, "We are looking at that question but have not come to any conclusions with our partners around the world."

The United States and other countries have been pressing Hun Sen to re-establish his coalition with Ranariddh's royalist party, set new elections for next year, allow political pluralism and a free press, and avoid the use of force.

In the past two days, Hun Sen has sought to legitimise his new government by calling for a quick convening of parliament, the holding of "free and fair" elections, and the protection of human rights and the press. On Tuesday he said elections would be held in May 1998.
Burns said, "The words are beautiful over the past 48 hours ... but whether or not he can match those words in reality with his actions is a very big test for him."

"And right now, he's not doing very well on that score, because there are still press reports -- a lot of press reports -- and a lot of other reports beyond the press that there have been people rounded up, both generals allied with Prince Ranariddh, politicians allied with him, and there have been executions," he added.
Burns also cited a statement by Hun Sen that Ranariddh was welcome to come back to Cambodia but would face trial if he did.
"Those are not the words of a statesman. And the threatened actions are certainly not consistent with what we would hope would take place in Cambodia," he said.
As for the drug-trafficking charges, he said, "To the best of our knowledge, we have no evidence that would link Hun Sen to drug trafficking."

In its 1997 report on drug trafficking around the world, the State Department said the most important step Cambodia could take "is to tackle the problem implicit in the accusations of high-level official corruption." It did not cite any names.
